commit_message:
[Vulkan] Refinement: planning, feature discovery, and device contracts (#24505)

This PR is the first cleanup and capability-enablement pass after the
Vulkan HAL rewrite landed. The rewrite made the driver functional, fast,
and aligned with the modern HAL queue model; this follow-up turns
several of the remaining large in-file policy clusters into named units
with explicit contracts, and adds feature discovery needed for the next
wave of Vulkan/SPIR-V targets.

The main design change is a cleaner split between **planning** and
**acting**: the driver now computes physical-device selection,
logical-device options, queue assignment, feature/extension enablement,
and external-device validation
before the live logical device is assembled. That makes the Vulkan HAL
easier to review, easier to test without a real GPU, and easier to
extend as Vulkan feature negotiation grows.

The PR also sharpens the capability model. Vulkan support is now
determined from enumerated extensions, queried features, and queried
properties. Function pointer availability is not used as a feature gate:
in static-loader or validation-layer configurations a symbol can exist
without the feature being legal to call, so feature availability must
come from the Vulkan device model itself.

## What changed

### Logical device creation is now plan-driven

Driver-owned creation and external `VkDevice` wrapping now share the
same logical-device planning path. The new `device_plan` unit computes
the durable facts needed by the logical device:

- queue role assignment for compute, transfer, and sparse binding;
- enabled HAL feature bits;
- enabled Vulkan device extension bits and extension-name arrays;
- enabled dispatch ABIs;
- `VkDeviceQueueCreateInfo` storage;
- the chained `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` feature structs used for
driver-owned `vkCreateDevice`;
- validation of externally supplied device features, extensions, and
queues.

This makes `logical_device.c` more of an apply step: consume a selected
physical-device snapshot, consume a device plan, create or wrap the
logical device, initialize queues, allocators, executable caches,
builtins, profiling, and file support.

### Device option policy is isolated

Device option defaults, string-pair parsing, dispatch ABI parsing, and
option validation now live in `device_options`. That pulls policy out of
logical-device construction and gives options focused coverage.

This also makes the dispatch ABI contract more obvious:

- `descriptor` remains the portable baseline executable ABI.
- `bda` is the optimized buffer-device-address ABI.
- `all` enables every supported ABI and lets the runtime select the best
match.

### Physical-device selection is isolated

Driver-owned physical-device selection now lives in
`physical_device_selection`. It has a small selector API with default,
id, and path modes.

The default selector only chooses devices satisfying the Vulkan HAL
baseline. Explicit id/path selectors distinguish “not found” from “found
but unsupported” so diagnostics are cleaner when a user asks for a
specific physical device.

### Request flags are no longer mixed with feature bits

The public Vulkan feature mask previously carried some behavior that is
not a Vulkan device feature. This PR splits those concepts:

- device features describe Vulkan features enabled on or supplied by the
logical device;
- request flags describe non-feature behavior such as validation layers,
debug utils, object names, and command labels.

That matters for external wrapping: a wrapped `VkDevice` can now
explicitly say which Vulkan device features and extensions are enabled,
separately from which debug/profiling behaviors IREE may use.

### Queue affinity resolves to queue lanes

Public queue-affinity masks are now resolved to concrete queue lanes at
logical device ingress. The plan records selected Vulkan queue
family/index pairs for compute, transfer, and sparse binding roles, and
the logical device exposes a small queue-lane model over those selected
queues.

This keeps today’s affinity API working while moving the internals
closer to the future HAL direction where queue affinity becomes an
opaque queue handle. The important part is that queue selection is no
longer an ad hoc mask test at every callsite: command buffers and
submissions are normalized against the live lane model before work
reaches the queue.

### Logical-device state has clearer representation boundaries

The logical device now groups queue state and profiling state into named
aggregates instead of spreading related fields through the whole object:

- queue selections, queue handles, mutexes, queue lanes, and public
affinity metadata live together;
- profiling recorder state, calibrated timestamp state, counters, and
clock alignment live together.

These are not flashy changes, but they make the big file materially
easier to reason about. Queue topology and profiling lifetime are now
visible as representation boundaries instead of being implicit in field
ordering.

### Debug utils are a real subsystem

`VK_EXT_debug_utils` handling now has a focused `debug_utils` unit. It
resolves which debug-utils capabilities are actually enabled for the
logical device:

- object names;
- command labels.

Command-buffer debug groups are recorded in the reusable HAL command
buffer and replayed as Vulkan command labels during native
command-buffer recording when command labels are available. Queue object
names are derived from the logical device id, queue role, and selected
Vulkan queue family/index.

This makes command streams more inspectable in Vulkan
debugging/profiling tools without putting debug-utils symbol checks
directly into hot logic.

## Unlocked features

### Cooperative matrix device profiles

The Vulkan HAL now recognizes `VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`, queries its
feature bit, captures its device properties, and exposes the cooperative
matrix property rows through a public query API:

```c
iree_hal_vulkan_device_query_cooperative_matrix_properties(...)
```

The property rows preserve Vulkan wire values for component types and
scopes so the compiler side can compare against SPIR-V/Vulkan enums
without inventing a parallel string schema.

Logical-device planning enables cooperative matrix support when the
extension and feature are present, validates wrapped devices that claim
the feature, and exposes query keys for both coarse support and property
details.

### `storageBuffer16BitAccess`

The physical-device snapshot now includes the Vulkan 1.1 feature chain,
and the device plan reports/enables `storageBuffer16BitAccess`. This
closes a gap in the scalar-storage feature set: 8-bit storage was
already visible through Vulkan 1.2 features, and 16-bit storage now
follows the same request/report model.

### `VK_KHR_shader_bfloat16`

The Vulkan HAL now recognizes `VK_KHR_shader_bfloat16` and
reports/enables its three feature bits when available:

- `shaderBFloat16Type`;
- `shaderBFloat16DotProduct`;
- `shaderBFloat16CooperativeMatrix`.

The implementation includes a local compatibility definition for
`VkPhysicalDeviceShaderBfloat16FeaturesKHR` so the runtime can build
while the checked-in Vulkan headers lag the extension. The fallback is
guarded by the extension macro, not by enum-token preprocessor checks.

External device wrapping validates the full contract: if a caller claims
any shader-bfloat16 feature bit, the wrapped device must also report
`VK_KHR_shader_bfloat16` in its enabled extension bitmask.

### Raw BDA SPIR-V with the Vulkan memory model

Raw BDA executable verification now accepts:

- `OpMemoryModel PhysicalStorageBuffer64 GLSL450`;
- `OpMemoryModel PhysicalStorageBuffer64 Vulkan`.

The Vulkan-memory-model form must also declare `OpCapability
VulkanMemoryModel`. That keeps the verifier permissive enough for modern
BDA modules without quietly accepting invalid SPIR-V.

### Feature and extension reporting is more complete

`iree-run-module --dump_devices` and Vulkan device queries now have
better coverage for the modern feature set:

- Vulkan 1.1 `storageBuffer16BitAccess`;
- Vulkan 1.2/1.3 baseline and scalar shader features;
- Vulkan memory model and device-scope memory model;
- cooperative matrix support and property rows;
- shader bfloat16 features;
- optional extension opportunities.

The docs now describe the Vulkan HAL baseline explicitly: Vulkan 1.3, a
compute queue, `timelineSemaphore`, `scalarBlockLayout`, and
`synchronization2`. Optional features remain opportunistic instead of
becoming part of the baseline.

## External wrapping contract

This PR makes external wrapping stricter and more explicit. A caller
wrapping an externally created `VkDevice` must provide:

- the Vulkan feature bits enabled on the device and usable by IREE;
- the recognized Vulkan device extension bits enabled on the device;
- non-feature request flags IREE may use;
- compute, transfer, and sparse-binding queue sets.

The wrap path verifies that claimed features are actually reported by
the physical-device snapshot and that extension-backed features also
have the corresponding enabled extension bit. This avoids the old
ambiguity where a feature-like flag could mean “requested,” “available,”
“enabled,” or “debug behavior,” depending on the callsite.

## Why this is worth doing now

The Vulkan HAL rewrite intentionally landed with a few large pieces
still in one place so the functional change could land without another
layer of churn. Now that the rewrite is in `main`, these follow-up
changes put the codebase in a better shape for real feature work:

- feature negotiation has a single plan-time home;
- external wrapping has a clear contract;
- queue topology is represented in a way that can evolve toward queue
handles;
- debug utils are isolated and testable;
- physical-device selection is no longer tangled with logical-device
assembly;
- new SPIR-V/Vulkan target features can be added as declarative snapshot
and plan bits instead of more `logical_device.c` branches.

The result is not just “more features.” It is a Vulkan HAL that is
easier to extend without guessing which of five nearby branches owns a
particular Vulkan invariant.

## Test coverage

This PR adds or expands focused unit coverage for the new boundaries:

- `api_test`
- `command_buffer_test`
- `debug_utils_test`
- `device_options_test`
- `device_plan_test`
- `physical_device_selection_test`
- `spirv_test`

Local focused ASAN run:

```bash
iree-bazel-test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:api_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:command_buffer_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:debug_utils_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:device_options_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:device_plan_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:physical_device_selection_test \
  //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/vulkan:spirv_test \
  --config=asan
```

Additional coverage during the stack included Vulkan subtree ASAN builds
and Windows/MSVC builds for the focused Vulkan API, device-plan, and
SPIR-V tests.

Vulkan HAL rewrite landed. The rewrite made the driver functional, fast,
and aligned with the modern HAL queue model; this follow-up turns
several of the remaining large in-file policy clusters into named units
with explicit contracts, and adds feature discovery needed for the next
wave of Vulkan/SPIR-V targets.

The main design change is a cleaner split between **planning** and
**acting**: the driver now computes physical-device selection,
logical-device options, queue assignment, feature/extension enablement,
and external-device validation
before the live logical device is assembled. That makes the Vulkan HAL
easier to review, easier to test without a real GPU, and easier to
extend as Vulkan feature negotiation grows.

The PR also sharpens the capability model. Vulkan support is now
determined from enumerated extensions, queried features, and queried
properties. Function pointer availability is not used as a feature gate:
in static-loader or validation-layer configurations a symbol can exist
without the feature being legal to call, so feature availability must
come from the Vulkan device model itself.

## What changed

### Logical device creation is now plan-driven

Driver-owned creation and external `VkDevice` wrapping now share the
same logical-device planning path. The new `device_plan` unit computes
the durable facts needed by the logical device:

- queue role assignment for compute, transfer, and sparse binding;
- enabled HAL feature bits;
- enabled Vulkan device extension bits and extension-name arrays;
- enabled dispatch ABIs;
- `VkDeviceQueueCreateInfo` storage;
- the chained `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` feature structs used for
driver-owned `vkCreateDevice`;
- validation of externally supplied device features, extensions, and
queues.

This makes `logical_device.c` more of an apply step: consume a selected
physical-device snapshot, consume a device plan, create or wrap the
logical device, initialize queues, allocators, executable caches,
builtins, profiling, and file support.

### Device option policy is isolated

Device option defaults, string-pair parsing, dispatch ABI parsing, and
option validation now live in `device_options`. That pulls policy out of
logical-device construction and gives options focused coverage.

This also makes the dispatch ABI contract more obvious:

- `descriptor` remains the portable baseline executable ABI.
- `bda` is the optimized buffer-device-address ABI.
- `all` enables every supported ABI and lets the runtime select the best
match.

### Physical-device selection is isolated

Driver-owned physical-device selection now lives in
`physical_device_selection`. It has a small selector API with default,
id, and path modes.

The default selector only chooses devices satisfying the Vulkan HAL
baseline. Explicit id/path selectors distinguish “not found” from “found
but unsupported” so diagnostics are cleaner when a user asks for a
specific physical device.

### Request flags are no longer mixed with feature bits

The public Vulkan feature mask previously carried some behavior that is
not a Vulkan device feature. This PR splits those concepts:

- device features describe Vulkan features enabled on or supplied by the
logical device;
- request flags describe non-feature behavior such as validation layers,
debug utils, object names, and command labels.

That matters for external wrapping: a wrapped `VkDevice` can now
explicitly say which Vulkan device features and extensions are enabled,
separately from which debug/profiling behaviors IREE may use.

### Queue affinity resolves to queue lanes

Public queue-affinity masks are now resolved to concrete queue lanes at
logical device ingress. The plan records selected Vulkan queue
family/index pairs for compute, transfer, and sparse binding roles, and
the logical device exposes a small queue-lane model over those selected
queues.

This keeps today’s affinity API working while moving the internals
closer to the future HAL direction where queue affinity becomes an
opaque queue handle. The important part is that queue selection is no
longer an ad hoc mask test at every callsite: command buffers and
submissions are normalized against the live lane model before work
reaches the queue.

### Logical-device state has clearer representation boundaries

The logical device now groups queue state and profiling state into named
aggregates instead of spreading related fields through the whole object:

- queue selections, queue handles, mutexes, queue lanes, and public
affinity metadata live together;
- profiling recorder state, calibrated timestamp state, counters, and
clock alignment live together.

These are not flashy changes, but they make the big file materially
easier to reason about. Queue topology and profiling lifetime are now
visible as representation boundaries instead of being implicit in field
ordering.

resolves which debug-utils capabilities are actually enabled for the
logical device:

- object names;
- command labels.

buffer and replayed as Vulkan command labels during native
command-buffer recording when command labels are available. Queue object
names are derived from the logical device id, queue role, and selected
Vulkan queue family/index.

debugging/profiling tools without putting debug-utils symbol checks
directly into hot logic.

easier to review, easier to test without a real GPU, and easier to
extend as Vulkan feature negotiation grows.

determined from enumerated extensions, queried features, and queried
properties. Function pointer availability is not used as a feature gate:
in static-loader or validation-layer configurations a symbol can exist
without the feature being legal to call, so feature availability must
come from the Vulkan device model itself.

- enabled dispatch ABIs;
- `VkDeviceQueueCreateInfo` storage;
- the chained `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` feature structs used for
driver-owned `vkCreateDevice`;
- validation of externally supplied device features, extensions, and
queues.

builtins, profiling, and file support.

### Device option policy is isolated

option validation now live in `device_options`. That pulls policy out of
logical-device construction and gives options focused coverage.

This also makes the dispatch ABI contract more obvious:

- `descriptor` remains the portable baseline executable ABI.
- `bda` is the optimized buffer-device-address ABI.
- `all` enables every supported ABI and lets the runtime select the best
match.

Driver-owned physical-device selection now lives in
`physical_device_selection`. It has a small selector API with default,

The public Vulkan feature mask previously carried some behavior that is
not a Vulkan device feature. This PR splits those concepts:

logical device;

explicitly say which Vulkan device features and extensions are enabled,
separately from which debug/profiling behaviors IREE may use.

logical device ingress. The plan records selected Vulkan queue
family/index pairs for compute, transfer, and sparse binding roles, and

opaque queue handle. The important part is that queue selection is no

ordering.

explicitly say which Vulkan device features and extensions are enabled,
separately from which debug/profiling behaviors IREE may use.

Public queue-affinity masks are now resolved to concrete queue lanes at
logical device ingress. The plan records selected Vulkan queue
family/index pairs for compute, transfer, and sparse binding roles, and
the logical device exposes a small queue-lane model over those selected
queues.

closer to the future HAL direction where queue affinity becomes an
opaque queue handle. The important part is that queue selection is no
longer an ad hoc mask test at every callsite: command buffers and
submissions are normalized against the live lane model before work
reaches the queue.

aggregates instead of spreading related fields through the whole object:

- queue selections, queue handles, mutexes, queue lanes, and public
affinity metadata live together;
- profiling recorder state, calibrated timestamp state, counters, and
clock alignment live together.

These are not flashy changes, but they make the big file materially
easier to reason about. Queue topology and profiling lifetime are now
visible as representation boundaries instead of being implicit in field
ordering.

resolves which debug-utils capabilities are actually enabled for the
logical device:

- command labels.

buffer and replayed as Vulkan command labels during native
command-buffer recording when command labels are available. Queue object
names are derived from the logical device id, queue role, and selected

[WebGPU] Add WebGPU HAL driver, WGSL compiler target, CTS, and sample. (#24463)

This adds the first end-to-end WebGPU target path for IREE: a compiler
backend that emits WGSL executables and a JavaScript-hosted HAL driver
that can submit those executables through the browser/Node WebGPU API
from a freestanding wasm32 runtime. Most gaps now exist in
infrastructure and hosting applications, with the HAL being largely
complete.

The important product boundary is that this is a WebGPU driver for the
Web platform, not an Emscripten port and not a native Dawn HAL. The C
runtime owns IREE's HAL object model, synchronization contracts, command
recording, executable metadata, and queue ordering. JavaScript owns the
ambient WebGPU objects, Promise completion delivery, and the import
module that maps integer wasm handles to real
GPUAdapter/GPUDevice/GPUBuffer/GPUQueue objects.

That split keeps the ABI narrow. All values crossing the wasm boundary
are integers or pointers into wasm linear memory. WebGPU objects are
represented as uint32 handles in a JS-side table, handle 0 is null, and
async WebGPU APIs complete through the JS proactor token ring introduced
by the wasm runtime commit. The C side never gets a raw JS object and
the JS side does not need to understand HAL resources beyond the
declared import ABI.

The driver uses an instruction-stream bridge instead of one wasm import
per HAL command. HAL command buffers and one-shot queue operations
compile into compact uint32 instruction blocks. JavaScript walks those
blocks in one bridge call, resolves dynamic bindings from a binding
table, reuses static bindings for cached recordings, batches encoder
commands, and submits pending GPUCommandBuffers at explicit
queue-surface boundaries. This makes the wasm/JS boundary a
command-stream boundary instead of a per-command overhead cliff.

The runtime queue contract follows WebGPU's actual execution model.
CPU-only operations can signal after their wait completes. GPU-submit
operations wait, encode/submit work, register
queue.onSubmittedWorkDone(), and signal HAL semaphores only when WebGPU
reports that submitted work is complete. Queue epochs and async
frontiers preserve causal ordering for downstream waits, while
submitted-provenance tracking keeps FIFO waits from adding unnecessary
host-side round trips.

WebGPU does not provide every primitive that IREE's HAL exposes
directly. The driver internalizes those gaps instead of pushing them
onto callers: fill uses a builtin WGSL compute shader, unaligned
copy/update paths fall back to a copy shader, executable loading creates
compute pipelines and bind group layouts from WGSL, and command
execution presents the usual HAL fill/copy/update/dispatch surface even
though WebGPU splits those operations across queue, encoder, and
compute-pass APIs.

The compiler side lowers through the existing SPIR-V path and translates
SPIR-V to WGSL with Tint/Dawn. The serialized executable format is
`webgpu-wgsl-fb`: a FlatBuffer containing WGSL shader modules plus
per-export metadata such as entry point names, workgroup sizes, binding
flags, constant counts, source/debug data, and the information the
runtime needs to create pipelines and bind groups. The target is
registered as the `webgpu` device and `webgpu-spirv` executable backend.

The initial runtime support contract is intentionally narrow. WebGPU
exposes one queue per device, so the driver currently routes through a
single queue while keeping queue state isolated enough for future
queue[N] shaping. The JavaScript inline host can validate WGSL and run
CTS-style entry points, but blocking C code cannot make JavaScript
Promises settle while the same wasm thread is waiting. CTS expected
failures document those blocking-completion cases instead of pretending
they are implemented.

This commit includes:

* A `webgpu` HAL driver with driver/device/allocator/buffer/semaphore/
executable objects, executable cache, FD-backed file helpers,
registration module, and public driver creation API.
* A C import ABI and JavaScript companion module for WebGPU object
handles, adapter/device requests, buffer mapping, command encoding,
pipeline creation, bind group creation, command-stream execution, cached
recordings, and queue.onSubmittedWorkDone() completion delivery.
* A compact WebGPU command ISA and builder that records HAL commands
into block-backed uint32 streams with dynamic/static binding slots and
automatic encoder begin/end insertion.
* Builtin WGSL fill/copy shaders used to provide HAL semantics where
WebGPU has no native command or requires stricter alignment than HAL
callers expose.
* A `webgpu-spirv` compiler plugin that reuses SPIR-V codegen, prepares
SPIR-V for WebGPU constraints, translates with Tint/Dawn, and packages
WGSL plus executable metadata into `webgpu-wgsl-fb`.
* HAL CTS wiring for the wasm32-wasi WebGPU path, including the Node
`webgpu` package loader, WASI preopen/output setup, and expected
failures for blocking-completion cases that the inline host cannot yet
satisfy.
* A WebGPU hello-world sample that builds a VMFB, dumps generated WGSL,
and validates that WGSL through Dawn's WebGPU implementation.
* Build-system integration for Bazel and CMake, including generated
CMake targets and explicit selection of the WebGPU SPIR-V compiler
target.

The CTS coverage exercises the runtime side under wasm32-wasi with the
JS WebGPU bridge. The passing coverage includes buffer, command buffer,
core, file, and queue CTS groups, with expected failures kept to the
operations that require a blocking C wait while JavaScript Promise
completions are still pending on the same inline host.

Together with the wasm runtime commit below it, this establishes the
first coherent WebGPU bring-up slice: IREE can generate WGSL for WebGPU,
package it in a HAL executable format, create WebGPU pipelines from that
executable, validate a hello-world shader end to end, and run meaningful
HAL CTS coverage through the same wasm/JS bridge that applications will
use. Future changes will build tooling and samples that run VMFB
programs.
